newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan newspaper reports 1986 Peru ambassador threat.
newsitem.headline: Japan newspaper reports 1986 Peru ambassador threat.

text.p: A major Japanese newspaper reported on Saturday that Japan's ambassador to Peru was threatened with kidnapping 10 years ago in a foretaste of the present hostage crisis in Lima.
The Asahi Shimbun said in the 1986 incident, then ambassador Tadatsuna Yabu was warned he would be killed unless he paid an advance ransom.
Japanese foreign ministry officials refused to comment on the report.

The Asahi, one of Japan's most respected newspapers, said that at the time of the incident Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement guerrillas -- the same group holding 103 hostages at the present Japanese ambassador's home -- were active in the country.
The newspaper quoted a foreign ministry source as saying although an embassy official, monitored by Peruvian police, turned up with $150,000 the extortionists did not appear.
"At the time, terror incidents were a daily occurrence, with employees of Japanese companies being shot, and so on," the newspaper quoted Yabu as saying. "You could feel the fear."
The Asahi, which did not give a specific date, said an advance ransom note was delivered in the summer of 1986 on the day of a banquet at the ambassador's residence.
The newspaper said about 700 guests, including top Peruvian bureaucrats, businessmen and diplomats were at the party.
A gala thrown by current ambassador Morihisa Aoki was targeted on December 17 when Marxist rebels took over his home during a birthday party for Emperor Akihito.
The 1986 note delivered to the residence threatened to kill the ambassador unless a ransom was brought to a Lima park. It was followed by an anonymous phone call repeating the threat.
The Asahi said the Japanese foreign ministry advised Yabu to flee the country if he felt his life was in danger but instead he contacted Peruvian authorities.
"I couldn't just run away and leave behind other Japanese who were living in fear. So the orders from Toyko left me in a dilemma..,." the Asahi quoted Yabu as saying.
The newspaper said a Japanese embassy official took a suitcase stuffed with $150,000 to the park rendezvous but the extortionists did not show up.
Peruvian and Japanese authorities never discovered who was behind the kidnap threat.
The newspaper added that guerrillas belonging to the more radical Shining Path movement were also involved at the time in attacks on Lima.
